html:
Athabaskan peoples, also called Dene, speak languages of a large family spread across western North America. On this map the label covers the northern interior of Alaska and northwestern Canada, the family's old heartland.

There are about 53 Athabaskan languages in three groups:

  • Northern, in interior Alaska and northwestern Canada, including Dena'ina, Gwich'in, Slavey and Chipewyan
  • Pacific Coast, in Oregon and northern California, including Hupa
  • Southern, or Apachean, including Navajo and the Apache languages

Athabaskan belongs to the wider Na-Dene family, with Eyak and, some argue, Tlingit. The southern peoples moved down from the far north and reached the American Southwest by about 1500; when they set out is debated.

Northern Athabaskan peoples lived as hunters and fishers in forest and tundra, living on caribou, moose and salmon. They travelled by birchbark canoe and snowshoe, in small family bands that moved with the seasons. In the 1700s and 1800s the fur trade drew them into dealings with the Hudson's Bay Company and, in Alaska, with traders of Russian America.

The name comes from Lake Athabasca in Canada, from a Cree word meaning "where there are reeds one after another". The scholar Albert Gallatin chose it for the family in the 1820s. Chipewyan is spoken over the largest area of any Native language in North America, and Navajo by the most people of any Native language north of Mexico.
sum: Athabaskan peoples, also called Dene, speak languages of a large family spread across western North America. On this map the label covers the northern interior of Alaska and northwestern Canada, the family's old heartland.
